'''Harley D. Rutledge''' (January 10, 1926 – June 5, 2006) was an American physicist and [[ufology|ufologist]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=September 30, 2023 |title=Did you know that Piedmont is the UFO capital of Missouri? |url=https://fox2now.com/news/missouri/did-you-know-that-piedmont-is-the-ufo-capital-of-missouri/ |access-date=December 6, 2023 |website=FOX 2 |language=en-US}}</ref> He earned a doctorate in solid-state physics from the [[University of Missouri]] and spent nearly two decades as chair of the physics department at [[Southeast Missouri State University]]. In the 1970s Rutledge directed Project Identification, a long-term field investigation of unidentified aerial phenomena in Missouri that was reported as the first sustained scientific study of UFOs. The project involved trained observers and technical instruments, and his findings were published in the 1981 book ''Project Identification: The First Scientific Study of UFO Phenomena''. Though widely recognized as a UFO expert and frequent media commentator, Rutledge emphasized that many sightings had conventional explanations.

== Life and career ==
Harley D. Rutledge was born in 1926 to Earl and Irene Hoagland Rutledge in [[Omaha, Nebraska]].<ref name="Rutledge Obit SE Missouri 2006-06-07">{{Cite web|date=June 7, 2006|title=Dr. Harley Rutledge|url=https://www.semissourian.com/obituaries/dr-harley-rutledge-1155702|url-status=live|website=[[Southeast Missourian]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20250910161047/https://www.semissourian.com/obituaries/dr-harley-rutledge-1155702|archive-date=September 10, 2025}}</ref> ''[[The Daily Nonpareil]]'' identified him as a native of southwest [[Iowa]].<ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15">{{Cite web|date=August 15, 1988|title=Man studies UFO mysteries|last1=Wilmarth|first1=Winnie|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/962136639/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[The Daily Nonpareil]]}}</ref> He attended high school in [[Red Oak, Iowa|Red Oak]], [[Henderson, Iowa|Henderson]], [[Macedonia, Iowa|Macedonia]], and [[Wales-Lincoln, Iowa]].<ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> Rutledge served in the [[United States Army]] from March 16, 1944, to May 3, 1946.<ref name="Rutledge Obit SE Missouri 2006-06-07" /> In 1954 he married Ruth Lootens at [[Taos, Missouri]].<ref name="Rutledge Obit SE Missouri 2006-06-07" /><ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> They had five children, including a son, Mark.<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> Rutledge was also active as a softball pitcher and bridge player.<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" />

Rutledge joined the physics department at [[Southeast Missouri State University]] in 1963.<ref name="Greaney Rutledge 2006-06-06" /> In 1966,<ref name="E-C Rutledge 1979-01-21" /> he completed his [[Ph.D.]] in [[solid-state physics]] at the [[University of Missouri]], and subsequently became professor and chairman of the Southeast physics department.<ref name="DAR Rutledge 2011-06-19">{{Cite web|date=June 19, 2011|title=UFO revival news interest in bizarre sightings|last1=Farley|first1=Donna|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/939287478/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[Rust Communications|Daily American Republic]]|page=2}}</ref><ref name="E-C Rutledge 1979-01-21" /><ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04">{{Cite web|date=December 4, 1977|title=Dedicated Watcher Of Sky Mysteries|last1=Creighton|first1=Jim|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/139119971/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]}}</ref> He remained chair for 18 years as of 1988.<ref name="Greaney Rutledge 2006-06-06" /><ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> Rutledge retired from teaching in 1992.<ref name="Greaney Rutledge 2006-06-06" />

In addition to his university post, Rutledge served as president of the [[Missouri Academy of Science, Mathematics and Computing]].<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08">{{Cite web|date=December 8, 1973|title=UFO Sightings Make Missouri Professor a Believer|last1=Brimble|first1=Phlllip S.|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/676479872/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[Kansas City Times]]}}</ref><ref name="E-C Rutledge 1979-01-21">{{Cite web|date=January 21, 1979|title=Professor describes lights in sky as 'miracles of physical science'|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/936675488/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[Rust Communications|Enterprise-Courier]]}}</ref> He was also a longtime member of the Southeast Missouri Astronomy Club.<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" />

Rutledge died on June 5, 2006, at the [[Missouri]] Veterans Home, aged 80.<ref name="Greaney Rutledge 2006-06-06">{{Cite web|date=June 6, 2006|title=Area UFO expert Dr. Harley Rutledge, 80, dies|last1=Greaney|first1=T. J. |url=https://www.semissourian.com/news/area-ufo-expert-dr-harley-rutledge-80-dies-1155552/|url-status=live|website=[[Southeast Missourian]]|archive-url=https://archive.today/20250910160729/https://www.semissourian.com/news/area-ufo-expert-dr-harley-rutledge-80-dies-1155552/|archive-date=September 10, 2025}}</ref>

==UFO research==
The ''Nonpareil'' and other newspapers described Rutledge as "an expert, appearing on numerous television and radio interviews and delivering papers to scientific bodies around the world".<ref name="WCJB Rutlidge 1988-03-31">{{Cite web|date=|title=UFOs Are Still Out There Says Dr. Harley Rutledge|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1122312804/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[Wayne County Journal-Banner]]}}</ref><ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> Challenged to explain sightings of [[Unidentified flying object|unidentified lights and luminous phenomena]] in the sky around [[Piedmont, Missouri]], Rutledge decided to subject these reports to [[Scientific method|scientific analysis]].<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> He organized a team of observers with college training in the physical sciences and assembled a wide range of equipment, including [[electromagnetic]] [[spectrum analyzers]], [[Reflecting telescope|Questar telescopes]], low- and high-frequency audio detectors, cameras, and a [[galvanometer]] to measure variations in the Earth's [[gravitational field]].<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> [[Oxford University]] later invited him to present his UFO findings.<ref name="DAR Rutledge 2011-06-19"|page=2 />

Of the UFO situation in Piedmont, Rutledge was quoted in 1977 by the ''[[St. Louis Post-Dispatch]]'': "I didn't like the way the Piedmonters were being treated by the media, and I was disturbed that some of the people there were truly frightened."<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> He framed his initial interest as humanitarian, telling the ''Nonpareil'' that he was motivated by how frightened retirees were at a rest home, and that women had begun arming themselves<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" /> in response to strange theories spread by "[[Pseudoscience|pseudo scientists]]" at the time.<ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> The ''[[St. Joseph News-Press]]'' reported that Rutledge entered the investigation as a skeptic.<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" /> He was also described as caring only about what "his data says".<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" />

Project Identification commenced in April 1973, logging several hundred hours of observation time.<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" /> The ''[[Kansas City Times]]'' and other contemporary reporting noted that Rutledge applied scientific scrutiny and standards to his UFO studies.<ref name="DAR Rutledge 2011-06-19"|page=2 /> It was described as the first scientific [[field study]] of UFOs conducted in real time, enabling Rutledge to calculate the objects' speed, course, position, distance, and size.<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08" /> With Drake Kambitch, a pilot and physics major at Southeast, and later other members of a growing team, the group searched for locations from the air every weekend and conducted field research in the area.<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> Rutledge said he first observed a UFO on May 11, 1973, while flying in a [[Cessna]] airplane with colleagues during an investigation.<ref name="E-C Rutledge 1979-01-21" /> He told the ''Times'' that he began the project as a skeptic but became convinced of the need for scientific research on the subject.<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08" /> The research team received financial support, including a $2,000 grant from the ''[[St. Louis Globe-Democrat]]''.<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08"|page=8b />

At Southeast, Rutledge taught a course on identified objects in the sky.<ref name="Rossi Rutledge 1979-01-21">{{Cite web|date=January 21, 1979|title=UFO observers|last1=Rossi|first1=Frank|authorlink1=|url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/1019606014/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[Columbia Daily Tribune]]}}</ref> He stated that many UFOs could be explained as normal aircraft or atmospheric conditions.<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08" /> By 1977, Rutledge reported having seen more than 140 UFOs,<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> a number he placed at 163 sightings by 1988.<ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> He discounted the likelihood of some UFOs being "hoaxes," arguing that only a government could afford the related expenses.<ref name="KCT Rutledge 1973-12-08"|page=8b />

Rutledge was notably uncomfortable in his UFO-related role.<ref name="Creighton Rutledge 1977-12-04" /> He reported becoming depressed for several weeks after his first observation of a UFO,<ref name="DNP Rutledge 1988-08-15" /> and believed he would be "ridiculed" and "ostracized" by colleagues as a result.<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22">{{Cite web|date=July 22, 1981|title=Scientist says he's seen UFOs 158 times|last1=Jakovac|first1= Lou |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/562065503/?match=1&terms=Harley%20Rutledge|website=[[St. Joseph News-Press]]}}</ref> According to the ''Enterprise-Courier'' of Missouri, he felt the term "UFO" carried "connotations of sensationalism".<ref name="E-C Rutledge 1979-01-21" /> Rutledge refused to accept a UFO sighting as valid unless he observed it himself.<ref name="Rossi Rutledge 1979-01-21" /> He emphasized that he did not advocate or believe in ideas such as the [[extraterrestrial UFO hypothesis]].<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" /> "I don't have the facts to prove that," he said. "Once I am known as an extraterrestrial believer, I will have to defend that for the rest of my life."<ref name="Jakovac Rutledge 1981-07-22" /> According to the ''Daily American Republic'' in 2011, his son Mark stated that his father never shared a conclusion of his theories before his death.<ref name="DAR Rutledge 2011-06-19"|page=2 /> "He wouldn't answer that question," Mark said, adding, "Scientists are not going to draw conclusions on things data won't support."<ref name="DAR Rutledge 2011-06-19"|page=2 />
